## Scope and motivation

MapBiomas Argentina Fuego Collection 1 will produce annual burned-area maps for all of Argentina over 1999–2025 using Landsat C2 SR. The pipeline relies on a per-observation (pixel-date) burn-probability classifier evaluated for **every Landsat scene** intersecting the territory and the time window. That prediction step is the cost driver: the model is applied many billions of times, so the structure must be **cheap to evaluate** in Google Earth Engine.

Collection 0 (Patagonia pilot) used a logistic regression with 40 terms per vegetation type, four fire-relevant indices (NBR, NBR2, MIRBI, NDVI), and a hand-picked interaction set that included custom annual min/max summaries and $\Delta$ values. Collection 1 keeps logistic regression — for the same compute reasons — but rebalances the design:

- **More focal flexibility**: 17 spectral features per observation instead of 4.
- **Previous-year context from MapBiomas**: replace custom-computed annual summaries with the official MapBiomas Argentina annual mosaic of year $y-1$, which provides phenologically informed composites at no extra preprocessing cost.
- **No deltas**: with rich pairwise interactions, monotonic effects and the inherent non-linearity of the logistic link absorb most of what $\Delta$ terms did in Collection 0. A 2-way interaction in $\eta$ already implies a roughly 3-way effect on the predicted probability.
- **Flexibility over interpretability**: this model is for prediction, not inference. Collinearity is acceptable and addressed by an elastic-net fit (tuning both $\lambda$ and $\alpha$).
- **Stratification**: one model per **region × vegetation type** (using the MapBiomas LULC of year $y-1$, reclassified into a few coarse classes), as in Collection 0.

The design constraint is roughly **200–300 terms per linear predictor**. Below 200 we lose flexibility; above 300 the GEE compute graph grows enough to slow down full-territory prediction without obvious gains.

## Why use the MapBiomas annual mosaic (instead of computing custom summaries)

In Collection 0 we computed our own per-pixel annual minimum and maximum of each fire index with a robust order-statistic rule. That was viable for one region × four indices but does not scale: doing the same over all of Argentina, for two years per focal year ($y-1$ in addition to $y$), with many more features, would multiply preprocessing cost considerably.

The MapBiomas Argentina annual mosaic already provides, for every year, a coherent set of pixel-level composites:

- median, dry-season median, wet-season median, minimum, and within-year standard deviation of the six optical bands;
- the same statistics for a broad set of vegetation and fire-relevant indices (NDVI, NDWI, EVI2, SAVI, GCVI, NDFI, SEFI, WEFI, ...);
- SMA endmember fractions (GV, GVS, NPV, soil, shade, cloud);
- topographic information.

Using this mosaic instead of recomputing custom summaries

- removes a heavy preprocessing step,
- ensures consistency with the LULC product used for stratification,
- offers seasonal composites (wet, dry) that we never had in Collection 0, and
- provides physically interpretable derived layers (NPV as a fuel-load proxy, NDFI as a fire/disturbance signal) we would not have built ourselves in the available time.

The trade-off is that we cannot freely define the summaries; we choose among what the mosaic exposes.

## Why these previous-year summaries (median, wet, sd)

A previous-year summary is useful only insofar as it describes the **stable spectral state** of the pixel — the baseline against which the focal observation is compared. Summaries that move sharply when the pixel itself was disturbed in $y-1$ are confounded by exactly the kind of signal we want to detect later in the time series.

We retain three summaries that meet this criterion, and apply the same rule to every previous-year variable in the proposal:

- $\text{med}$ — robust central tendency over the year. Insensitive to a single fire event unless the fire affected a large fraction of the year's images.
- $\text{wet}$ — median of wet-season images. The wet season in Argentina precedes the fire season, so a fire in year $y-1$ generally occurs *after* the wet-season composite is laid down. The wet composite is therefore the most fire-robust baseline available in the mosaic.
- $\text{sd}$ — within-year standard deviation. A measure of spectral variability that contextualizes change: pixels with naturally high $\text{sd}$ should be judged against a more permissive threshold for burn detection.

We deliberately exclude:

- $\text{dry}$. The dry season *is* the fire season, so a fire in $y-1$ contaminates the dry-season composite in the same direction as the future fire we are trying to detect: dry-season NDVI drops, dry-season SWIR rises. Using $\text{dry}$ as a baseline biases the model toward calling already-burned pixels "unburned baseline".
- $\text{amp}$ (amplitude = max − min). Either a fire or a normal phenological cycle inflates amplitude, so this summary cannot separate "stable strongly-seasonal vegetation" from "vegetation that burned last year". Worst of both worlds.
- $\text{min}$, $\text{max}$. In Collection 0 these supported $\Delta$ features; without $\Delta$ terms here, they are redundant with what $\text{med} + \text{sd} + \text{wet}$ already convey, with worse robustness.

## Notation

| Subscript | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| $X_t$ | Value of feature $X$ at the focal observation (pixel-date) |
| $X_{\text{med}}$ | MapBiomas mosaic **median** of $X$ in year $y(t) - 1$ |
| $X_{\text{wet}}$ | MapBiomas mosaic **wet-season median** of $X$ in year $y(t) - 1$ |
| $X_{\text{dry}}$ | MapBiomas mosaic **dry-season median** of $X$ in year $y(t) - 1$ |
| $X_{\text{sd}}$ | MapBiomas mosaic **within-year standard deviation** of $X$ in year $y(t) - 1$ |

The bare optical-band symbols (BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2) refer to surface reflectance after harmonization to the OLI domain (Roy et al. 2016).

## Spectral feature equations

The base focal feature set comprises **17 features**: six optical bands and 11 indices. The canonical team proposal (see §) extends this to **21** by adding AFRI, kNDVI, EVI2, and NIRv.

| Group | Feature | Definition |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Optical | BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 | Surface-reflectance bands |
| Fire | $\text{NBR}$ | $(\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR2}) \,/\, (\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR2})$ |
| Fire | $\text{NBR2}$ | $(\text{SWIR1} - \text{SWIR2}) \,/\, (\text{SWIR1} + \text{SWIR2})$ |
| Fire | $\text{MIRBI}$ | $10\,\text{SWIR2} - 9.8\,\text{SWIR1} + 2$ |
| Fire | $\text{NDVI}$ | $(\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) \,/\, (\text{NIR} + \text{RED})$ |
| Tasseled-cap | $\text{TCB}$ | $0.3029\,\text{BLUE} + 0.2786\,\text{GREEN} + 0.4733\,\text{RED}$ <br> $+\ 0.5599\,\text{NIR} + 0.5080\,\text{SWIR1} + 0.1872\,\text{SWIR2}$ |
| Tasseled-cap | $\text{TCG}$ | $-0.2941\,\text{BLUE} - 0.2430\,\text{GREEN} - 0.5424\,\text{RED}$ <br> $+\ 0.7276\,\text{NIR} + 0.0713\,\text{SWIR1} - 0.1608\,\text{SWIR2}$ |
| Tasseled-cap | $\text{TCW}$ | $0.1511\,\text{BLUE} + 0.1973\,\text{GREEN} + 0.3283\,\text{RED}$ <br> $+\ 0.3407\,\text{NIR} - 0.7117\,\text{SWIR1} - 0.4559\,\text{SWIR2}$ |
| Aux. moisture | $\text{NDMI}$ | $(\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR1}) \,/\, (\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR1})$ |
| Aux. snow | $\text{NDSI}$ | $(\text{GREEN} - \text{SWIR1}) \,/\, (\text{GREEN} + \text{SWIR1})$ |
| Aux. sparse veg | $\text{SAVI}$ | $\left[(\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) \,/\, (\text{NIR} + \text{RED} + L)\right]\,(1 + L)$, with $L = 0.5$ |
| Aux. open water | $\text{NDWI}$ | $(\text{GREEN} - \text{NIR}) \,/\, (\text{GREEN} + \text{NIR})$ |
| Aux. aerosol-free | $\text{AFRI}$ | $(\text{NIR} - 0.5\,\text{SWIR2}) \,/\, (\text{NIR} + 0.5\,\text{SWIR2})$ |
| Aux. veg. kernel | $\text{kNDVI}$ | $\tanh\!\left(\text{NDVI}^2\right)$ |
| Aux. enhanced veg | $\text{EVI2}$ | $2.5\,(\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) \,/\, (\text{NIR} + 2.4\,\text{RED} + 1)$ |
| Aux. NIR veg | $\text{NIRv}$ | $\text{NIR} \times \text{NDVI}$ |

Notes: Tasseled-cap coefficients are Baig et al. (2014) for Landsat 8 OLI. MIRBI is in the raw Trigg & Flasse (2001) orientation; it *increases* after fire (opposite sign of NBR, NBR2, NDVI). NDWI here is McFeeters (1996), distinct from NDMI (Gao 1996). The four canonical-team additions: AFRI is AFRI-2100 (Karnieli et al. 2001, Eq. 11a), the 2.1 µm / 0.5-coefficient variant — preferred over AFRI-1600 because the 2.1 µm band penetrates smoke and aerosol better and correlates more tightly with NDVI; kNDVI uses the RBF kernel $k(x,x) = \tanh(\text{NDVI}^2)$ (Camps-Valls et al. 2021); EVI2 is the blue-band-free EVI variant (Jiang et al. 2008); NIRv is the near-infrared reflectance of vegetation (Badgley et al. 2017).

Previous-year variables used beyond the six optical bands are taken directly from the MapBiomas mosaic. For reference:

- $\text{NDVI}$: same formula as the focal NDVI.
- $\text{NDWI}$: same formula as the focal NDWI.
- $\text{NPV}$: non-photosynthetic vegetation fraction from spectral mixture analysis. Proxy for fine-fuel load (dead biomass).
- $\text{NDFI}$: Normalized Difference Fraction Index (Souza et al. 2005), $\text{NDFI} = (\text{GV}_s - (\text{NPV} + \text{SOIL})) \,/\, (\text{GV}_s + \text{NPV} + \text{SOIL})$, where $\text{GV}_s$ is shade-normalized green vegetation.

## Canonical proposal — 300 terms

The linear predictor for the logistic regression has **300 terms per region × veg-type cluster**, organized in six blocks. The model is

$$\Pr(y_{c,t} = 1) = \sigma\!\left(\alpha_{k[c]} + \sum_{j=1}^{300} \beta_{j,k[c]}\, x_{j,c,t}\right),$$

where $k[c]$ is the vegetation cluster of pixel $c$ in year $y-1$ and $\sigma$ is the logistic function.

### Block 1 — focal raw (17)

The 17 focal features above, used as main effects.

### Block 2 — previous-year raw (30)

Six optical bands plus four index variables, each carried with the three previous-year summaries:

| Variable | Summaries | Count |
|:---|:---|---:|
| BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 18 |
| NDVI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 3 |
| NDWI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 3 |
| NPV | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 3 |
| NDFI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 3 |
| | | **30** |

### Block 3 — focal × focal pairwise (136)

All unordered pairs of the 17 focal features: $\binom{17}{2} = 136$.

This block carries most of the model's flexibility. Representative terms include
$\text{NIR}_t \times \text{SWIR2}_t$ (the raw constituents of NBR, in product form, supplying curvature),
$\text{NBR}_t \times \text{MIRBI}_t$ (concordance of two fire signatures),
$\text{TCW}_t \times \text{NDMI}_t$ (moisture redundancy),
$\text{RED}_t \times \text{SWIR1}_t$ (drought / bare-soil discrimination), etc.

### Block 4 — same-band previous × focal (24)

Each previous-year summary of a band is multiplied by the same band measured at the focal observation. The product encodes "how unusual is the focal value given the local baseline".

| Band (prev) × Band (focal) | Summaries | Count |
|:---|:---|---:|
| BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 18 |
| NDVI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 3 |
| NDWI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{sd}$ | 3 |
| | | **24** |

Example terms: $\text{NIR}_t \times \text{NIR}_{\text{wet}}$, $\text{NDVI}_t \times \text{NDVI}_{\text{sd}}$, $\text{SWIR2}_t \times \text{SWIR2}_{\text{med}}$.

### Block 5 — prev context × focal fire indices (45)

Each of the four "context" prev-year variables (NDVI, NDWI, NPV, NDFI), in each of the three summaries, multiplied by each of the four focal fire indices (NBR, NBR2, MIRBI, NDVI):

$$4 \times 3 \times 4 = 48,$$

minus the 3 $\text{NDVI}_{\text{stat}} \times \text{NDVI}_t$ terms already in Block 4 ⇒ **45**.

These interactions encode the central modeling claim of this design: **the meaning of a focal fire-index value depends on the previous-year vegetation context**. A low $\text{NBR}_t$ in a high-NPV, low-NDFI pixel (heavy dead biomass, recently disturbed) is much more likely to be a fire than the same $\text{NBR}_t$ in a low-NPV, high-NDFI pixel.

Example terms: $\text{NPV}_{\text{wet}} \times \text{NBR}_t$, $\text{NDFI}_{\text{sd}} \times \text{MIRBI}_t$, $\text{NDWI}_{\text{med}} \times \text{NBR2}_t$.

### Block 6 — prev context × focal fire bands (48)

Each of the four "context" prev-year variables (NDVI, NDWI, NPV, NDFI), in each of the three summaries, multiplied by each of the four focal fire-relevant optical bands (RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2):

$$4 \times 3 \times 4 = 48.$$

No overlap with Block 4 (which crosses each band with its *same-band* prev summary) or Block 5 (which crosses prev context with focal fire *indices* rather than raw bands).

These extend the context-dependence logic of Block 5 to the raw fire-sensitive bands: the meaning of focal RED, NIR, SWIR1 and SWIR2 also depends on previous-year vegetation context, and raw bands carry information that the NBR / NBR2 / MIRBI indices necessarily compress by combining pairs. SWIR2 is the single most fire-discriminating band; its product with NPV (fine-fuel proxy) or NDFI (recent-disturbance signal) is a direct candidate for high informativeness.

Example terms: $\text{NPV}_{\text{med}} \times \text{SWIR2}_t$, $\text{NDFI}_{\text{wet}} \times \text{NIR}_t$, $\text{NDVI}_{\text{sd}} \times \text{SWIR1}_t$.

### Term-count summary

| Block | Description | Count |
|:---|:---|---:|
| 1 | Focal raw | 17 |
| 2 | Prev raw | 30 |
| 3 | Focal × focal pairwise | 136 |
| 4 | Same-band prev × focal | 24 |
| 5 | Prev context × focal fire indices | 45 |
| 6 | Prev context × focal fire bands | 48 |
| | **Total** | **300** |

## Canonical team — 427 terms

The **canonical team** proposal extends the canonical design in two directions simultaneously:

1. **Four additional focal predictors** (AFRI, kNDVI, EVI2, NIRv) raise the focal feature set from 17 to **21**.
2. **Dry-season median** ($\text{dry}$) added as a fourth previous-year summary alongside $\text{med}$, $\text{wet}$, $\text{sd}$.

**On the inclusion of $\text{dry}$:** §3 argues that the dry season coincides with the fire season, so a $y-1$ fire contaminates the dry composite in the same direction as the signal to detect. That argument stands for pixels that *did* burn in $y-1$. For the majority of pixels — which did not burn the previous year — dry-season composites capture peak senescence, deciduous phenology, and end-of-season fuel state, all potentially informative signals. Including $\text{dry}$ lets the elastic net make the call: for non-burned pixels it can assign positive weight; for pixels whose other features already indicate prior-year disturbance, regularization can downweight it. The bias risk is real but bounded, and empirical validation should adjudicate.

**On the four new focal predictors:**

- **AFRI** (AFRI-2100): $(\text{NIR} - 0.5\,\text{SWIR2}) / (\text{NIR} + 0.5\,\text{SWIR2})$. Reduces aerosol interference relative to pure-NIR ratios by weighting the 2.1 µm SWIR2 band; the SWIR is largely transparent to smoke, so under aerosol-affected scenes AFRI tracks the true NDVI far better than NDVI itself (Karnieli et al. 2001). The 2.1 µm / 0.5-coefficient form (Eq. 11a) is preferred over the 1.6 µm / 0.66 form (Eq. 11b): it penetrates the atmospheric column better and correlates more tightly with NDVI ($r=0.98$ in Karnieli et al.).
- **kNDVI**: $\tanh(\text{NDVI}^2)$. Applies a radial-basis-function kernel to NDVI, expanding the effective dynamic range in dense canopy where linear NDVI saturates. Injects a smooth non-linearity into Block 1 without requiring an explicit quadratic interaction term.
- **EVI2**: $2.5\,(\text{NIR} - \text{RED}) / (\text{NIR} + 2.4\,\text{RED} + 1)$. Corrects for soil background and canopy reflectance anisotropy without requiring the blue band; better behaved in open shrubland and semi-arid strata where NDVI and kNDVI compress.
- **NIRv**: $\text{NIR} \times \text{NDVI}$. Near-infrared reflectance of vegetation, proportional to absorbed photosynthetically active radiation; works as a fractional green-canopy signal in mixed pixels and is near-orthogonal to bare-soil brightness in the NIR–red plane.

### Block 1 — focal raw (21)

The 17 canonical focal features plus AFRI, kNDVI, EVI2, and NIRv.

### Block 2 — previous-year raw (40)

Same 10 variables as canonical, each carried with four summaries:

| Variable | Summaries | Count |
|:---|:---|---:|
| BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 24 |
| NDVI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 4 |
| NDWI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 4 |
| NPV | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 4 |
| NDFI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 4 |
| | | **40** |

### Block 3 — focal × focal pairwise (210)

All unordered pairs of the 21 focal features: $\binom{21}{2} = 210$.

The 74 new pairs (those involving at least one of AFRI, kNDVI, EVI2, NIRv) include physically motivated combinations: AFRI $\times$ MIRBI (concordance of two SWIR-based fire signals), kNDVI $\times$ NBR (non-linear greenness against burn ratio), NIRv $\times$ SWIR2 (photosynthetically active canopy fraction against the primary fire band), EVI2 $\times$ TCW (canopy structure against moisture).

### Block 4 — same-band previous × focal (32)

Eight variables × four summaries × same-band focal:

| Band (prev) × Band (focal) | Summaries | Count |
|:---|:---|---:|
| BLUE, GREEN, RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 24 |
| NDVI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 4 |
| NDWI | $\text{med}, \text{wet}, \text{dry}, \text{sd}$ | 4 |
| | | **32** |

### Block 5 — prev context × focal fire indices (60)

Four context variables (NDVI, NDWI, NPV, NDFI) × four summaries × four focal fire indices (NBR, NBR2, MIRBI, NDVI):

$$4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64,$$

minus the four $\text{NDVI}_{\text{stat}} \times \text{NDVI}_t$ terms already in Block 4 ⇒ **60**.

### Block 6 — prev context × focal fire bands (64)

Four context variables × four summaries × four focal fire bands (RED, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2):

$$4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64.$$

No overlap with Block 4 (same-band) or Block 5 (fire indices vs. fire bands).

### Term-count summary

| Block | Description | Count |
|:---|:---|---:|
| 1 | Focal raw | 21 |
| 2 | Prev raw | 40 |
| 3 | Focal × focal pairwise | 210 |
| 4 | Same-band prev × focal | 32 |
| 5 | Prev context × focal fire indices | 60 |
| 6 | Prev context × focal fire bands | 64 |
| | **Total** | **427** |

The 127-term increase over canonical (300 → 427) comes primarily from the expanded pairwise block (Block 3: +74) and from the fourth summary across all blocks (+49, matching the rich (+ dry) delta in the Alternatives table). The GEE block-multiply pattern keeps the compute graph at ~15 nodes regardless: Block 3 produces a 210-band image in a single `.multiply()` call, identical in node count to the canonical 136-band version. The main operational cost increases are a larger coefficient array (~43 % more floats in the `.reduce()` step) and longer R fitting time.

## Alternatives

A slim or rich variant is available without changing the block structure:

| Variant | Change relative to canonical | Total |
|:---|:---|---:|
| **Slim** | Drop NPV and NDFI everywhere (raw and crosses) | 246 |
| **Canonical** | as described above | **300** |
| **Rich** | Add 15 prev-optical-median pairs (new block 7) | 315 |
| **Rich (+ dry)** | Add $\text{dry}$ as a 4th prev summary across Blocks 2, 4, 5, 6 | 349 |
| **Canonical team** | Add AFRI, kNDVI, EVI2, NIRv focal + $\text{dry}$ summary | **427** |

- The **slim variant (246)** is appropriate if validation later shows NPV/NDFI add little incremental skill, or if compute pressure forces shrinking the linear predictor. NPV and NDFI contribute 6 prev-raw terms (Block 2), 24 prev × focal-fire-index terms (Block 5), and 24 prev × focal-fire-band terms (Block 6) — 54 in total.
- The **rich variant (315)** adds the 15 prev-optical-median pairs $\text{B}_{\text{med}} \times \text{B}'_{\text{med}}$ with $\text{B} \neq \text{B}' \in \{\text{BLUE}, \dots, \text{SWIR2}\}$, giving the model a representation of the *position* of the pixel in previous-year color space; this is useful if some veg-type clusters in non-linear regions of that space. Consider this variant only if validation in some region × veg-type cluster is poor with the canonical model.
- The **rich (+ dry) variant (349)** restores the dry-season median as a fourth prev summary alongside $\text{med}$, $\text{wet}$, $\text{sd}$, across every block that uses prev summaries: Block 2 (+10 prev-raw), Block 4 (+8 same-band crosses), Block 5 (+15: $4 \times 1 \times 4$ minus the new NDVI×NDVI overlap with Block 4), Block 6 (+16: $4 \times 1 \times 4$) — 49 terms in total. This deliberately reintroduces the summary excluded from canonical because the dry season is the fire season (see "Why these previous-year summaries"). The motivation is that for pixels that did *not* burn in $y-1$, dry-season composites are still well-defined and may add information the wet/median pair misses (peak senescence, deciduous response, end-of-season fuel state); the model can in principle learn to discount dry-season terms when other signals indicate $y-1$ disturbance. Consider only if validation suggests the canonical baseline is under-resolved at the end of the wet season → dry season transition, and accept the bias risk on pixels that burned the previous year.

## Computational considerations

The model is evaluated for every Landsat observation in Argentina over 1999–2025. The implementation pattern below keeps the GEE compute graph at roughly **15 nodes regardless of the term count**, by relying on the fact that `.multiply()` between two multiband images is a single server-side node that produces one multiband image with elementwise products band-by-band.

### Pattern

The key idea: instead of looping `for each term: select two bands, multiply, accumulate` (which produces O(n) chained server-side nodes), express each interaction *block* as one multiply between two parallel band lists.

```js
// ---- Step 1: build the two source images with distinct band names ----
// Focal features get a "_t" suffix to disambiguate from prev-year bands.
var focal = computeFocal(landsat).rename(focalNames);     // 17 bands, e.g. "NBR_t"
var prev  = mbMosaic.select(prevBandsRaw)
                    .rename(prevNames);                   // 30 bands, e.g. "NDVI_wet"

// ---- Step 2: stack into a single multiband image ----
var X0 = focal.addBands(prev);                            // 47 bands

// ---- Step 3: build each interaction block in ONE multiply ----
// pairs_a, pairs_b are parallel arrays of length 136
// pairs_names = ["NBR_t__NDVI_t", "NBR_t__MIRBI_t", ...]
var pairs    = X0.select(pairs_a).multiply(X0.select(pairs_b))
                                  .rename(pairs_names);    // 136 bands

var sameband = X0.select(sameband_a).multiply(X0.select(sameband_b))
                                    .rename(sameband_names); // 24 bands

var cross    = X0.select(cross_a).multiply(X0.select(cross_b))
                                  .rename(cross_names);    // 45 bands

var cross2   = X0.select(cross2_a).multiply(X0.select(cross2_b))
                                  .rename(cross2_names);   // 48 bands

// ---- Step 4: assemble the full 300-band predictor ----
var X = X0.addBands(pairs).addBands(sameband).addBands(cross).addBands(cross2);

// ---- Step 5: weighted sum + sigmoid ----
// coefValues is an array of 300 floats matched to coefNames (= X.bandNames()).
var coefImg = ee.Image.constant(coefValues).rename(coefNames);
var eta     = X.multiply(coefImg).reduce(ee.Reducer.sum()).add(alpha);
var p       = eta.multiply(-1).exp().add(1).pow(-1);       // sigmoid
```

### Why this is small

The whole construction has roughly:

| Operation | Nodes |
|:---|:---|
| Compute focal features (1 expression call) | 1 |
| Select & rename prev mosaic | 1 |
| Stack | 1 |
| Four block multiplies (`pairs`, `sameband`, `cross`, `cross2`) | 4 |
| Concatenate blocks | 1 |
| Coefficient constant image | 1 |
| Multiply by coefficients | 1 |
| Reduce-sum | 1 |
| Add intercept | 1 |
| Sigmoid | 3 |
| | **~15** |

The graph size does not grow with the number of terms. A 500-term version would have the same node count as a 50-term one. This is the same pattern Collection 0 used implicitly for its 40-term model; we are just being explicit about it.

### Practical wrinkles

- **Band-name uniqueness.** Because focal and prev are stacked into one image, names must be globally unique. The `_t` / `_med` / `_wet` / `_sd` suffix convention handles this; `addBands` will throw if two sources share a band name. Worth keeping that strict and asserting it once in code.
- **Four name-list pairs.** `(pairs_a, pairs_b)`, `(sameband_a, sameband_b)`, `(cross_a, cross_b)`, `(cross2_a, cross2_b)`, with parallel `*_names` outputs. These should be generated programmatically from the constants (`OPTICAL_BANDS`, `FIRE_INDICES`, `TC_INDICES`, `EXTRA_INDICES`, plus the prev subset), not hand-written. The same generator emits the canonical band-name list that gets serialized with coefficients.
- **Coefficient JSON.** Store as `{"NBR_t__NDVI_wet": 0.123, ...}` plus a separate `{"NBR_t": {"mean": ..., "sd": ...}, ...}` for the pre-fit standardization, plus the intercept. At prediction time, JS reads the JSON, builds `coefNames` and `coefValues` in matching order, and feeds Step 5. No positional fragility.
- **Projections.** Reproject the MapBiomas mosaic to the Landsat scene projection once at the top, so the multiply chain is not silently triggering reprojections per node.
- **Export tasks, not interactive.** Run from `Export.image.toAsset`; interactive evaluation has tighter limits.

### What about SMA / unmixing cost?

SMA-derived layers (NPV, NDFI, GV, etc.) are *consumed* as ordinary bands of the MapBiomas mosaic — they are not recomputed per Landsat scene. MapBiomas runs the per-pixel constrained-least-squares unmixing once per year and stores the results as raster bands; we just `.select()` them. **Zero per-pixel array operations on our side.** This is the strongest reason to use the mosaic instead of computing our own annual summaries.

Tasseled-cap is a fixed linear combination of the six optical bands, one `.expression()` for three bands, equivalent in cost to a band ratio. Not a concern.

## Fitting

Coefficients are estimated locally in R with `glmnet` (elastic net):

- both $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ tuned by cross-validation;
- CV folds **stratified by region × veg-type × burned** and **grouped by training point**, so observations belonging to the same point fall in the same fold (avoids over-optimism from temporal autocorrelation within a point's time series);
- fit with `standardize = TRUE` (the default). `glmnet` internally centres and scales each column of the design matrix to mean 0 and sd 1, fits the elastic-net path in that scale, and **returns coefficients on the original feature scale**. No manual back-transformation is needed and the JSON written for GEE prediction is keyed by feature name with values applicable to raw inputs.

Per-cluster active-set size is a useful diagnostic: if it lands near the full 252 in every cluster the regularization is binding and a rich variant may help; if it lands well below, the canonical design is over-parameterized for that cluster and the slim variant is preferable. Coefficients near zero can still be carried into GEE — there is no operational reason to prune unless we want to shrink the compute graph.

### Numerical precision

The 300-term design has features with vastly different scales: focal optical bands in $[0, 1]$, MapBiomas mosaic bands as integers in $[0, 10000]$, and products of two mosaic bands in $[0, 10^8]$. This raises two precision concerns: (a) does the *fit* suffer from the scale disparity, and (b) does float32 *prediction* in GEE introduce noticeable error?

**At fit time.** `glmnet`'s internal standardization handles the scale disparity. The optimizer sees a well-conditioned design matrix; coefficients are returned on the original scale. No action required.

**At prediction time.** GEE uses float32, which provides roughly 7 significant digits of *relative* precision regardless of magnitude. The gap between consecutive representable floats grows with the value: ~$10^{-7}$ near 1, ~$10^{-3}$ near $10^4$, ~$0.06$ near $10^6$. The relevant question is whether the linear predictor $\eta$ can be computed accurately enough.

Two regimes:

- **$|\eta|$ large**: the sigmoid saturates to 0 or 1 within $5 \times 10^{-5}$ for $|\eta| > 10$. Precision in $\eta$ is irrelevant.
- **$\eta$ near 0**: the contributions summing to $\eta$ are by definition not all of large magnitude (otherwise their sum would not be small). Float32 sums of ~300 contributions of order $O(1)$ have accumulated rounding error of order $\sqrt{300} \cdot 10^{-7} \approx 10^{-5.5}$, giving error in predicted $p$ also of order $10^{-5}$. Negligible.

The one scenario in which precision could matter is **catastrophic cancellation between a large intercept and a large sum of positive contributions**: e.g., an intercept of $-15000$ balancing a $+15000$ sum of products from un-centred prev-mosaic bands. Each contribution would have ~3 digits of precision (gap of $10^{-3}$ near $10^4$), so 300 terms could accumulate error of order $0.02$ in $\eta$ and ~$0.005$ in $p$. Even this worst case is dwarfed by downstream sources of error (K=5 median smoothing, annual summaries, region-growing). The practical conclusion is that **no rescaling at prediction time is required**.

### Optional precision insurance — prev-mosaic centering

Should validation ever reveal a precision-related issue, the simplest cure is a single elementwise centering of the prev mosaic before forming any products:

```js
// means computed once from training data and stored in the coefficient JSON
var meansImage = ee.Image.constant(prevMeans).rename(prevNames);
var prevCentered = prev.subtract(meansImage);    // ONE 30-band node
var X0 = focal.addBands(prevCentered);
// ... rest of the pipeline unchanged ...
```

This is a 30-band subtraction, performed once per tile and reused across all focal Landsat scenes within the year. Earth Engine's compute graph is a DAG with common-subexpression deduplication (Gorelick et al. 2017): if `prevCentered` is assigned once and referenced many times downstream, it occupies a single node in the graph; the subtraction is then executed once per output tile regardless of how many focal scenes consume it. The cost is essentially zero.

If centering is enabled, the coefficient JSON must additionally store the 30-element vector of prev-band means (computed over the training observations of the corresponding region × veg-type cluster), and the fit must be re-run on the centered prev features so coefficients match the centered scale.

### Multinomial extension

A natural future extension is to predict more classes than burned/unburned — e.g., {unburned, burned, cloud, water, ash, drought, recent-deforestation, agriculture} — addressing the major sources of false positives in Collection 0 directly. `glmnet` supports multinomial logistic regression with elastic-net regularization out of the box via `family = "multinomial"`. The option `type.multinomial = "grouped"` applies a group-lasso penalty so a feature is either active across all class equations or pruned from all of them — usually the right choice for a small-$K$, large-$p$ classifier.

In GEE, prediction with $K$ classes computes $K$ linear predictors (one per class, with the baseline class fixed at $\eta = 0$) and applies a softmax instead of a sigmoid. The same block-multiply pattern applies; only the final aggregation step changes. Compute cost at prediction is $\sim K \times$ the binary case.

The `mgcv::gam` family `multinom(K = ...)` is an alternative if non-linearities in a small number of features prove important (smooth terms `s(x)` for those features, parametric for the rest), but lacks regularized feature selection — not the right primary tool for a 252-term predictor.

## Summary of design choices

- **Logistic regression**: cheap at prediction time, trivial to implement in GEE, sufficient when richly parameterized.
- **17 focal features + all focal pairs (153 terms)**: captures non-monotonic fire signatures and disambiguates fire from drought, ash, deforestation, defoliation and agriculture, which were the dominant confusion sources in Collection 0.
- **30 prev-year raw + 117 prev × focal interactions (147 terms)**: turns the focal classifier into a *context-aware* classifier without requiring per-pixel temporal change features.
- **Elastic net at fit time**: handles collinearity, picks among redundant features, and produces a sparse-ish coefficient vector at no cost to GEE prediction.
- **No deltas, no annual min/max, no $\text{dry}$/$\text{amp}$**: the first two are absorbed by interactions and the logistic non-linearity, the last two are confounded by the very signal we want to detect.
